title: Spacewalk Success: Astronauts Install Next‑Gen ISS Solar Arrays, Boosting Station Power Efficiency
body:
Astronauts aboard the International Space Station completed a marathon spacewalk on Thursday, installing the first set of next‑generation iROSA solar arrays that will dramatically boost the station’s power output. The six‑hour extravehicular activity (EVA) saw the crew secure and connect three of the new roll‑out solar panels, marking a pivotal step in a multi‑year effort to modernise the station’s aging power system. With the iROSA modules now fully integrated, the ISS will generate up to 20 percent more electricity, extending its operational life and supporting an expanding slate of scientific experiments.

The installation was the culmination of a program that began with the launch of the first iROSA units in 2021. Those early panels were temporarily attached to the station’s existing solar wings to test their performance in orbit. Over the past two years, engineers on the ground refined the design, addressing challenges such as thermal expansion, vibration during launch, and the need for a compact stowage configuration that could be deployed by hand in microgravity. The latest EVA, carried out by NASA astronauts Shane Kimbrough and Thomas Pesquet, alongside ESA astronaut Matthias Maurer, involved the removal of protective covers, the precise alignment of the new arrays with the station’s power bus, and the meticulous routing of cables through pre‑installed conduit pathways.

Beyond the immediate power boost, the iROSA upgrades represent a strategic shift toward modular, replaceable hardware on the ISS. The original solar arrays, installed during the station’s construction in the late 1990s, are now well beyond their design life and have suffered degradation from prolonged exposure to the harsh space environment. By adopting a roll‑out architecture, each iROSA panel can be launched in a compact form factor and then unfurled like a banner, eliminating the need for large, rigid truss structures. This approach not only reduces launch mass and cost but also simplifies future maintenance—new panels can be swapped out as needed without extensive disassembly of the station’s core components.

The successful deployment also underscores the growing international collaboration that keeps the ISS operational. While NASA provided the primary funding and technical oversight, contributions came from the European Space Agency, the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency, and commercial partners such as SpaceX, which delivered the hardware to the station aboard a cargo Dragon spacecraft. This cooperative model has become increasingly important as the station approaches the end of its originally planned 15‑year service window, with extensions now pushing its operational horizon into the late 2020s and potentially beyond.

Looking ahead, the iROSA program is slated to continue through at least 2027, with additional panels scheduled for installation during upcoming EVAs. Each new array will further increase the station’s electrical capacity, enabling more power‑intensive experiments in fields ranging from materials science to biotechnology. Moreover, the upgraded power infrastructure lays the groundwork for future commercial and research modules that may attach to the ISS, as well as for the eventual transition to a new generation of low‑Earth‑orbit habitats. As the station’s solar sails unfurl, the promise of a brighter, more capable orbiting laboratory moves one step closer to reality.
